None of the East‑Coast states that both touch the Atlantic Ocean and have a land area larger than Ohio’s  ≈ 40,945 sq mi had a higher‑education attainment rate (bachelor’s degree or higher) that exceeded Ohio’s 49.5 % rate in 2019, according to the Center for American Progress (CAP).

**East‑Coast states touching the Atlantic with larger land area than Ohio**

| State | Land area (sq mi) | CAP 2019 adult college‑degree attainment (%) |
|-------|------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| New York | ≈ 47,126 | 48 % |
| Pennsylvania | 44,820 | 44 % |
| North Carolina | 48,718 | 39 % |
| Georgia | 57,915 | 31 % |
| Florida | 54,243 | 43 % |

**Ohio**

| State | Land area (sq mi) | CAP 2019 adult college‑degree attainment (%) |
|-------|------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Ohio | ≈ 40,945 | 49.5 % |

(Ohio’s 49.5 % figure comes from the 2021 Ohio attainment report [Ohio Attainment Report 2021, “2019 educational attainment rate of 49.5 percent”] and the CAP values are taken from the Center for American Progress **Adult Attainment Report** interactive data (the PDF snapshot shows NY 48 %, PA 44 %, NC 39 %, GA 31 %, FL 43 % [CAP Adult Attainment 2019 snapshot]).

Since every CAP adult‑attainment figure above is lower than Ohio’s 49.5 %, **no Atlantic‑coast state with land area greater than Ohio has a higher‑education attainment rate exceeding that of Ohio in 2019**.

Ohio is the 34th-largest state by area, at 44,825 sq mi (116,100 km2), and the seventh-most populous state, with a population of nearly 11.9 million. Its capital and most populous city is Columbus. Other urban areas include the major metropolitan cities of Cleveland and Cincinnati, alongside Dayton, Akron, and Toledo.

Ohio derives its name from the Ohio River that forms its southern border, which, in turn, originated from the Seneca word ohiːyo', meaning "good river", "great river", or "large creek".[15][16] Its geography is varied, with rolling glaciated plains across most of the state, rugged unglaciated hills in the southeastern Allegheny Plateau, and Lake Erie coastline to the north. At the time of European contact, the area known as the Ohio Country was inhabited by Algonquian and Iroquoian nations, and was contested among Native American tribes, Britain, and France. Following American independence, Ohio was organized as part of the Northwest Territory and achieved statehood in 1803. Ohio was the first state admitted under the Northwest Ordinance and the first post-colonial free state admitted to the union.[3][17]
Historically known as the heart of American industry, Ohio has the third-largest manufacturing sector and second-largest automobile production in the U.S.; it also has a large agriculture sector.[18] The state has shifted to a more information and service-based economy in the 21st century, ranking seventh in GDP as of 2025.[19] Tourism in Ohio is driven by attractions such as Cedar Point, the National Museum of the United States Air Force and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, as well as recreation areas including Cuyahoga Valley National Park and 76 state parks. Ohio is nicknamed the "Buckeye State" after its Ohio buckeye trees.[11] It is also known as the "Mother of Presidents", having been the birthplace of seven U.S. presidents,[20] and the "Birthplace of Aviation", as the Wright brothers designed and built the world's first successful airplane in Ohio before its first flight in North Carolina.[21]
